notes.title: Chapter map: Modality & model-specific prompting

headings.text: 🌳 Portable prompt, or a rendering per family?

notes.html:
How the prompt changes with who reads it and what the job is. Note 102 separates what moves between model families from what doesn't; 103 is the smallest family. 106 and 105 are the two task shapes with the most prompt design in them; 107 and 108 are smaller task shapes; 104 and 109 change the input itself. Read each arrow as a sentence: model-family differences sharpens in small models. The neighbouring model-upgrade process is in the cross-section links below.

Blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another section. This section has no CORE note.

Reading order:102 model-family differences106 extraction105 code generation107 summarisation108 classification at scale104 multimodal103 small models109 cross-lingual

Owners

Idea Owner note

Image labels, image cost as a prompt concern, placement as a thing to test 104 multimodal

A legal absent value; separating close fields; a span per value and the presence check 106 extraction
Faithful before short; a span per claim in a summary 107 summarisation, applying 106's check

Moved on 31 Oct 2026: the coding loop diagram in note 105 was dropped for the Agentic note that owns it. The schema comparison in note 106 was dropped for note 36. The per-provider table in note 102 moved to this map. Older text of every note is in 08-Prompt-engineering/_superseded/11-Modality & Model-Specific Prompting/.

Portable prompt, or a rendering per family?

  • 1️⃣ One prompt (102): if a family starts failing the eval after an upgrade, go down the tree.
  • Settings adapter (102): if the request runs and quality still differs, the gap wasn't only the API.
  • 🎨 Rendering per family (102): if the task statement itself has to change, you have forked prompts and can't compare families.
  • Keep it off that family (115): if the cost saving outweighs the measured loss, accept the loss and record it.

The other notes are task shapes, not alternatives: you don't choose between extraction and summarisation, so they have no tree.

At a glance

Note What it adds to the prompt Extra cost per request Fails as What enforces it

103 Small models fewer words, one job per call possibly more calls one prompt doing several jobs nothing: a request

105 Code generation symptom, pattern, scope, runnable check more calls per task "done" with nothing run CI, a harness hook, the apply step
106 Extraction legal null, field descriptions, spans span tokens fabrication that parses schema for shape; span check for presence
107 Summarisation a span per claim span tokens unsupported claim that reads well span check for presence
108 Classification closed labels, tie-break, way out one label; thinking if on forced wrong label enum
109 Cross-lingual a stated output language none wrong language; quality gap by language a language detector on the output, if you add one

Lineage

Read from each provider's page on 31 Oct 2026. Guidance is each provider's own, for its own models. Current model names change too often for this table: use the Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini model pages. Schema mechanisms are in section 04's Landscape (read 11 Oct 2026).

Modality and task facts

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: the task is yours and travels; how it's rendered belongs to the reader. Sort each difference into what you change in the prompt and what you change in code, then let the eval decide.
  • The two most-confused pairs: a style difference vs a feature difference (102: a request the model weighs, against a rule the API applies) · schema-valid vs grounded (106: a well-formed record, against one whose values are in the document).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: note 102's anatomy block and rule table, note 105's edit-format table, note 106's anatomy block and Break it, and this map's tree.
  • Cross-section links: a family change in production is model-upgrade migration; the guarantee under extraction is JSON mode and schemas; the size of model per request is model routing. Content gaps: no note on prompting for audio or video input (the voice pillar covers speech agents, not prompting a model with audio); none on prompting image generation; none on translation as a task; Anthropic PDF input was not re-read here.

notes.title: Model-Family Differences — One Task Spine, a Rendering per Family
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompting best practices · OpenAI: prompt engineering · Google: prompt design strategies · Sclar et al. 2023: sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design

TL;DR

What moves between model families is the task spine: the job, the examples, the output contract, the eval set. What doesn't move is the rendering: how regions are marked, which slot carries your authority, which request settings exist. Sort every difference into style (changed in the prompt, proved by the eval) or feature (changed in code, because the API decides it). What each provider says today is dated in the chapter map's Landscape.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:spine (task, examples, contract, golden set)renderer per familysettings adapter per familysame golden set on eachfix that rendering

─no regression─▶ one spine version, one variant per family

Recall

Prompt Answer
What moves between families? Task, examples, output contract, eval set. Not markers, slots or settings.
Style or feature: why sort them? Style is changed in the prompt; a feature is changed in code.
When is one portable prompt right? When every family passes the same eval, so variants would only add upkeep.

The idea

A contract-extraction prompt was tuned on one family. The team moves it to a cheaper one by changing the model name. The first request returns a 400 on a prefilled turn and a thinking budget. They delete both, the JSON parses, and accuracy on one field falls. Nobody can say whether the model or the prompt caused it, because one string does two jobs.

Split it. The spine says what the task is; the rendering says how this family is told. Now a regression points at one layer. You think family differences are about delimiters; the ones that cost you are the ones the API enforces. Everything else is a request, and the eval decides whether it matters.

The trade: per-family renderings cost upkeep and an eval run per family; one shared string costs you the ability to say why quality moved.

How it works

Each difference between families falls into one of four kinds, and each kind has its own remedy.

Rule What actually happens
Syntax: slots and markers Authored text goes in a different slot per API, and open models have their own turn tokens. A wrong template fails silently.
Features: what the API accepts A parameter can be rejected or ignored by model. A 400 is the good case; an ignored setting says nothing.
Guidance: house style Providers recommend different orders and example counts for their own models: a starting point, attributed and dated.
Defaults: behaviour you never asked for Length, hedging, refusals and reasoning change by model. They surface only in a golden-set diff.

Size inside a family can matter as much: see small-model prompting. How much reasoning to prompt for is owned by reasoning models.

Evolution

Lineage:Oct 2023 accuracy shown to move with format aloneDec 2024 developer messages on OpenAI's reasoning modelsby Oct 2026 Claude's thinking controlled by effort, not a token budgetby Oct 2026 sampling settings dropped or ignored on the newest models of all three providers
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). All three providers publish guidance by model or generation.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Style matters less as models accept each other's structure; features keep diverging. What won't change: the eval per family, and the task kept apart from its rendering.
  • Checked on: vendor guides read 31 Oct 2026. No cross-family benchmark of house styles was found, so this is vendor advice, not a measured result.

Code

The prompt, split by what moves and what doesn't.

① TASK         Extract the parties and the termination clause.      ← spine: same everywhere
② CONSTRAINTS  Only what the contract states; null if absent.       ← spine
③ EXAMPLES     2 filled records                                     ← spine; test the count
④ CONTEXT      {{contract}} inside tags, or under a heading         ← rendering: the marker varies
⑤ OUTPUT       schema sent through the API where it exists          ← feature, not wording

The same task as one string, and as a spine with a renderer.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) one string; the model name is the only change regions ①–③ shared; ④ and ⑤ rendered per family
On the input the same contract, on a new family a 400 on old settings; then one field regresses, cause unknown settings set by the adapter; a regression is pinned to one rendering
Fails as carried-over settings, untraceable regression —
The one edit — separating the spine from the rendering, so one thing changes at a time

Measure it

  • Offline: the same golden set per family against the current production pair; a variant ships on its own family's numbers, never on an average across families.
  • In production: quality, refusals and output length per (spine version, family, model). A shift on one family alone is a rendering or model change.
  • Enforced by: the renderer and adapter in code for slots and settings; a request lint in CI for known-rejected parameters. House style is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: The task moves between families; the rendering doesn't. I keep one spine, the task, examples, contract and golden set, and render it per family. Style I change in the prompt and prove with the eval. Features I change in code, because the API decides them. The sharpest edge today is settings and scaffolds written for an older model.

Q · Mechanism — Why does the same text behave differently on two families? Each family was trained on different data, and its API turns your messages into a different token sequence, so even "system" isn't one thing across them. Identical words are a different conditioning prefix. That is why a swap needs an eval, and why optimised prompts don't transfer either.

Q · Trade-off — One portable prompt, or one per family? The simpler rung is one prompt: if it passes the eval on every family you run, stop there. Climb to renderings only on a measured gap. Keep variants honest by sharing the spine and putting the family in the version key. If the task statement itself diverges, you can no longer compare families.

Pitfalls

  • "An old reasoning scaffold is harmless on a newer model"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it helped before, and extra instructions look free.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: OpenAI's reasoning guide says it can hinder, and as of Oct 2026 Anthropic warns that pushing reasoning into the response can draw a refusal on some models.
    ↳ Think instead: delete the scaffold first, then add back only what the eval asks for.
  • 🧙 Folklore: "Claude likes XML, GPT likes Markdown"
    ↳ Why it spread: each vendor's guide shows its favourite in the examples, and screenshots did the rest.
    ↳ What the evidence says: as of Oct 2026 OpenAI and Google both accept Markdown or XML, Anthropic recommends tags, and no cross-family benchmark was found.
    ↳ Do instead: mark boundaries consistently, then test a change of marker on your own set.
  • Not the same: a style difference vs a feature difference
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both show up as "this prompt needs changing for that model".
    ↳ Difference: style is a request the model weighs. A feature is decided by the API: a schema, a rejected parameter, a thinking control.
    ↳ Think instead: if deleting the sentence changes nothing the API checks, it's style; budget effort on features first.
  • Don't write variants for a task any model passes.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: per-family prompts feel rigorous, and vendor guides invite tuning.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you maintain three copies of something that never regresses, and each change now needs three eval runs.
    ↳ Do instead: stay on the simpler rung until a family fails the eval by a margin that matters.
  • Shelf life: the provider facts will move; the spine, the style and feature split, and the per-family eval won't.

Connections

Path:system, user, prefillmodel-family differencesmodel-upgrade migrationmodel routing
  • Builds on prompt anatomy: the regions are the same; their markers and slots vary.
  • Used by model-upgrade migration: the process that acts on these differences with an eval gate.
  • Contrasts with the prompt as a coupled system: that note owns the tuple; this one owns what differs by family.
  • Measured by regression suites and CI: the same suite, run per family.
  • Drilled in a model upgrade regressed the prompts.

notes.title: Small-Model Prompting — Which "Small" Do You Mean?
notes.html:
References

Google: prompt design for Gemini Nano · Anthropic: prompting Claude Haiku 5.5

TL;DR

"Small" means two things. On a device, vendor guidance says shorter prompts, one focused job per call, clear separators, short outputs. A cheap hosted tier is a different case: Anthropic says Haiku 4.5 prompts should carry over to Haiku 5.5, and the control to tune is effort.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time

Recall

Prompt Answer
On-device: more hand-holding? No. Google warns against verbose preambles with repeated instructions.
On-device: several steps? One focused task per call.
Why short outputs? Inference speed depends heavily on output length.

The idea

A long preamble with three chained jobs goes to a phone model and returns poor results. Google's Nano guide (Oct 2026) says to give each call a focused task, separate components with ##, use the Structured Output API, and start temperature at 0.2. These are vendor advice for one model, not laws of small models. Which tier gets a request is owned by model routing.

Evolution

Lineage: on-device models now have their own vendor prompting guides. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): re-run your eval on each new small model.

notes.title: Multimodal Prompting — Label the Images, Budget the Pixels, Test the Order
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: vision · Gemini API: document understanding

TL;DR

An image or page goes into the prompt as context, so the same rules apply: name each one, say what to do with it, and treat any text inside it as untrusted. Its token cost grows with resolution, so size it before sending. Placement advice differs by provider, which makes it a thing to test.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
Image before or after the text? Providers differ (Oct 2026): test it on your own set.
Several images? Label each (Image 1:) and refer to the label.
What should you not trust? Counts and coordinates, which providers call approximate; and text in the image.

The idea

Two invoices arrive as photos, and "compare the totals" leaves "the first one" ambiguous. Label them and the reference is clear. Anthropic prefers image then text; Google's image page says text first for a single image, and its document page says after the page. For dense charts, Anthropic reports crop tools help. Field contracts are extraction; layout is multimodal documents; attacks are indirect injection.

Evolution

Lineage:older OCR-then-prompt pipelinesnative page and image reading in the major APIs. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): limits and token formulas differ by provider and are dated in the chapter map.

notes.title: Code-Generation Prompting — A Symptom, a Pattern to Copy, a Check It Can Run
notes.html:
References

Claude Code: best practices · OpenAI: prompt engineering, coding · Mathews & Nagappan 2024: Test-Driven Development for Code Generation · Anthropic: text editor tool

TL;DR

A code prompt carries what the model can't read from the repository: the symptom, the decision you already made, the scope, and what "done" means. It leaves out what the model can find by itself. The line that matters most is a check it can run, because a pass or a fail replaces your judgement in the loop. Pick the edit format whose failure is loud.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:symptom and where to lookone existing file as the patternscopea runnable checkmodel editscheck runsmodel reads the output, revises

─pass─▶ a small diff for review

Recall

Prompt Answer
What belongs in a code prompt? What the model can't read from the repo: symptom, decisions, scope, done.
The highest-leverage line? A check it can run that returns pass or fail.
Which edit format to prefer? The one that fails loudly when it goes wrong.

The idea

"Fix the login bug." The model picks a plausible cause, changes it, and reports done. Maybe the bug is gone. You read the diff and become the test suite.

Now say what the model can't know: the failure follows a session timeout, the cause is near token refresh, retries follow an existing file, one folder may change, and a named test must pass. The model can now close the loop itself.

Older advice said to load the right files and watch the window. Anthropic's Claude Code page (Oct 2026) now lists that as advice to stop following, because models read a repository well and windows are large. The skill moved from choosing files to stating what isn't in them.

The trade: the check and the scope cost you minutes and each run costs more calls; without them you pay in review. The prompt is a request; only a check outside the model is enforced.

How it works

Anthropic's page (Oct 2026) gives two tests for each line: could the model find this by reading the code, and would it go and look? If both are yes, leave it out.

Rule What actually happens
Point, don't describe One real file carries conventions you'd forget to write down.
A check returns pass or fail A test, a build, a linter or a script: the model reads the result and iterates.
Name the scope Off-limits folders and "no new libraries" are decisions the code can't show.

The loop around this prompt is owned by coding agents.

Evolution

Lineage:Feb 2024 tests in the prompt raise solve rates on function-level benchmarks2025 hooks and skills move rules into harnessesby Oct 2026 vendor advice drops "manage the window"
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). The vendor's own page keeps a list of advice it has retired.
  • Stronger-model test: partly: better models need less pointing. What won't change: a model can't read a decision that isn't in the repo.
  • Checked on: Mathews & Nagappan (2024) used GPT-4 and Llama 3 on MBPP and HumanEval, function-level. Repository-scale advice here is vendor guidance, not a measured gain.

Code

A prompt for one bug.

① TASK         Login fails after the session times out. Find the cause and fix it.  ← symptom, not a guess
② CONTEXT      Start at token refresh in src/auth/.                                 ← where, no file dump
③ EXAMPLES     Follow the retry pattern in src/http/client.py.                      ← a real file as the shape
④ CONSTRAINTS  Change src/auth/ only. No new libraries.                             ← your decisions
⑤ OUTPUT       Add a failing test first; done means `pytest tests/auth` passes.     ← a result it can read

The same bug as a one-line request.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) fix the login bug regions ①–⑤ above
On the input a timeout bug in a large repo a plausible fix elsewhere, unrelated edits, "done" with nothing run a reproduced failure, a change inside scope, a passing command
Fails as wrong problem solved; unverified claim —
The one edit — ⑤ a runnable check

The edit format is an output contract: choose it by how it fails.

Format Size of output When it goes wrong
Whole file the file a dropped function still applies cleanly: silent
Unified diff the change an invented context line won't apply: loud
Exact-match replace or patch tool the change no match returns an error your code feeds back: loud

Break it: a two-function file, a whole-file rewrite that lost tax(), and a diff with one wrong context line.

import subprocess                                    # whole.patch: a rewrite that dropped tax()
for name in ("whole", "bad", "good"):                # bad.patch: one invented context line
    r = subprocess.run(["git", "apply", "--check", f"../{name}.patch"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(name, r.returncode, r.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1:])
# look for: which patch git refuses
# naive belief predicts: the damaging rewrite is the one rejected

Run with git 2.54: whole exits 0, bad exits 1 with "patch does not apply", and good exits 0. After whole applies, tax is gone from the module.

Measure it

  • Offline: share of a fixed task set whose held-back tests pass, against the one-line request; compare diff size too.
  • In production: patch-apply failures per format, reverts, and reports of "done" with no check in the transcript.
  • Enforced by: CI and a harness stop hook for the check, and the apply step for the format. Scope is a request unless permissions or a hook block the write.

Interview

30-second answer: Code prompting is mostly stating what the model can't read from the repo: the symptom, my decisions, the scope, and what done means. The strongest line is a check it can run, so it iterates without me. I point at a real file as the pattern. And I choose an edit format that fails loudly, because a whole-file rewrite that drops a function applies cleanly.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a runnable check beat better wording? Wording shapes the first attempt. A check gives the model a signal outside its own judgement, so it reads the failure and revises. Without one, "looks done" is the only stopping condition.

Q · Trade-off — Diff or whole file? For an edit to an existing file, a diff or an exact-match replace: output scales with the change, and a mismatch errors. It needs the model to have read the file, and a repair path. Whole-file output is the simpler rung: it suits new files or pervasive changes; add a check that public names survive.

Pitfalls

  • "More context means better code"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: less to guess should mean fewer mistakes.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the model reads the repo well, so pasted files mostly repeat what it would find. Decisions never written down are the real gap.
    ↳ Think instead: write what it can't read; point at the rest.
  • "The tests pass, so the change is right"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: green is the signal you asked for.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a model aimed only at green can hard-code expected values; Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026) names this and gives a prompt against it.
    ↳ Think instead: say "solve it for all valid inputs", and review the assertions, not only the colour.
  • Not the same: a prompted check vs an enforced check
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both read as "the tests must pass".
    ↳ Difference: in the prompt, the model decides when it's satisfied. In a hook or CI, your code refuses to finish.
    ↳ Think instead: if a rule can't have exceptions, move it out of the prompt.
  • Don't plan or write a spec for a one-line change.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: plan-first worked on a big change.
    ↳ What goes wrong: review goes on a plan no longer than the diff, at the cost of more calls.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rung: if one sentence describes the diff, ask for the edit.
  • Shelf life: tool names and retired advice change fast. "State what can't be read" and "fail loudly" won't.

Connections

Path:output-format specificationcode-generation promptingcoding agentsharness mechanics
  • Builds on prompt anatomy: the same regions, with a file as the example.
  • Owned elsewhere: harness mechanics (Agentic) covers hooks, permissions and sub-agents.
  • Contrasts with self-refine loops: there the critic is a model; here it's a test.
  • Attacked by indirect prompt injection: code comments and tool output carry text into the window.
  • Measured by component vs end-to-end eval: task success, not one generated function.

notes.title: Prompting for Extraction — Make Absence Legal, Make Every Value Point at Its Source
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: structured outputs · OpenAI: structured outputs · Anthropic: reduce hallucinations · Gemini API: document understanding

TL;DR

A schema guarantees the record's shape and says nothing about whether the values came from the document. So extraction prompting spends its words on what a schema can't do: a legal way to say "not there", a description that tells close fields apart, and a source span per value that your code can check. A required slot with no value in the document gets an invented one, perfectly typed.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:schema holds the shapefield descriptions separate close fieldsnull is legal"state only what is there"a source span per valuecode looks for the span in the documentflag for review

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does every optional field need? A legal absent value, and an instruction to use it instead of guessing.
What does a source span give you? A check code can run, and a fast review.
What does a span check miss? A real span that fills the wrong field.

The idea

A scanned invoice has no printed number, an illegible total, and a "Remit to: Northbridge Bank" line. The schema makes every field required. The record arrives valid, with a made-up number, a guessed total, and the bank as vendor. Nothing fails.

The schema closed every exit except inventing. Open one: null is allowed and the instruction says to use it. Then ask for the span each value came from, so a value that isn't in the document becomes visible.

The trade: spans cost output tokens on every call and a check in your code; without them a fabricated value looks as sound as a true one. Null is a request. The span lookup is enforced, for presence only.

How it works

Each edit closes one route to a wrong value. The guarantee itself is owned by JSON mode and schemas, field meaning by output-format specification.

Rule What actually happens
Absence is a value A field that can be missing is nullable, and the prompt says use null.
Close fields get a sentence "Effective date, which may differ from the signature date" sits beside the slot being filled.
Spans are copied, not summarised A verbatim span can be searched for in the source by plain code.
Derived values are not extracted "Never compute" keeps arithmetic out of a read; your code does the sums.

Extraction from retrieved chunks is owned by structured output from RAG; reading tables out of a file by table and figure extraction.

Evolution

Lineage:Nov 2023 JSON modeAug 2024 schema-enforced output2024–25 enforcement across providers moves the problem from parsing to whether values are true
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Anthropic's structured-output page presents extraction as a named use.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Better reading lowers the error rate; the need for a legal absent value stays. What won't change: a shape guarantee isn't a truth guarantee.
  • Checked on: Anthropic's hallucination page, read 31 Oct 2026, recommends allowing "I don't know" and quoting first, with no figure; measure it per field.

Code

The field descriptions are part of the prompt.

① TASK         Extract the invoice fields from <doc>.                   ← one job
② CONSTRAINTS  State only what <doc> says. Absent: null. Never compute. ← makes absence legal
③ OUTPUT       vendor_name: issuing entity, not the remit-to bank       ← separates close fields
④ OUTPUT       issue_date: YYYY-MM-DD, or null                          ← format inside the field
⑤ OUTPUT       evidence: field name → exact span from <doc>             ← gives code something to check
⑥ CONTEXT      <doc>{{document}}</doc>                                  ← untrusted: data

The same invoice, pleading against contract.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Extract vendor, number, date, total. Return valid JSON. regions ②–⑤, with null allowed in the schema
On the input no number printed, illegible total, a remit-to line invented number, guessed total, wrong entity, all valid null, null, the issuing entity, with spans
Fails as fabrication that parses —
The one edit — ② making absence legal: enforcement alone gives the same fabrications in the right shape

Break it: the schema and the span check on scripted records.

DOC = "Calder Freight Ltd, Unit 7. Remit to: Northbridge Bank. Total: [illegible]."
SCHEMA = {"vendor": str, "invoice_number": (str, type(None)), "total": (float, type(None))}
def schema_ok(r): return all(isinstance(r[k], t) for k, t in SCHEMA.items())
def not_in_doc(r, ev): return [k for k, v in r.items() if v is not None and ev.get(k, "\0") not in DOC]
fabricated = {"vendor": "Northbridge Bank", "invoice_number": "INV-0001", "total": 1840.0}
honest = {"vendor": "Calder Freight Ltd", "invoice_number": None, "total": None}
print(schema_ok(fabricated), not_in_doc(fabricated, {"vendor": "Northbridge Bank", "invoice_number": "INV-0001"}))
print(schema_ok(honest), not_in_doc(honest, {"vendor": "Calder Freight Ltd"}))
# look for: the fabricated record passing the schema
# naive belief predicts: a schema-valid record is a correct record

Run on Python 3.15: both pass the schema; the fabricated one is flagged on invoice_number and total, the honest one on nothing. vendor isn't flagged, because the bank's name is in the document: a span proves presence, not that it fills the right field.

Measure it

  • Offline: per-field exact match against gold records, plus the fabrication rate on fields known to be absent, against the format-pleading prompt.
  • In production: per-field null rate and span-miss rate per prompt version. A null rate falling to zero after a change means the model has stopped admitting absence.
  • Enforced by: a schema for shape and your span check for presence. The right field is a request only, checked by the eval.

Interview

30-second answer: Extraction is schema design more than instruction writing. The schema holds the shape. The prompt adds a legal null, so the model isn't forced to invent; a description that separates close fields; and a source span per value that my code can check. I score per field against gold records. Structured output solved parsing, not truth.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a nullable field reduce fabrication? A required slot must be filled, and decoding offers no way to leave it empty, so the only choice is which value to invent. Nullable gives a legal path and the instruction points at it. Neither is enforced: they raise the odds that the model takes the honest exit.

Q · Trade-off — One call for thirty fields, or several? The simpler rung is one call: cheaper, faster, and fields inform each other. Split only on measured, field-specific loss, and split by where fields come from, header fields apart from clause fields, so each call gets narrower context as well as a shorter schema. The price is assembly and an extra round trip.

Pitfalls

  • "Structured output solved extraction"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the parse errors vanish overnight.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it solved parsing. Invented values arrive perfectly typed, so they're harder to notice than before.
    ↳ Think instead: a schema makes a wrong value well-formed. Measure values per field.
  • "A source span proves the value is right"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the text really is in the document.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a true span can fill the wrong field. In Break it the remit-to bank passes as vendor because its name is in the document.
    ↳ Think instead: a span check proves presence; field assignment still needs gold records.
  • Don't use a model where a parser works.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one extraction prompt seems to handle every format.
    ↳ What goes wrong: fixed-layout forms, CSVs and EDI gain only cost, latency and a new failure mode.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rung: parse deterministically, and spend the model on variable layouts and natural language.
  • Don't make a field required to keep the schema clean.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nullable types mean more checks in downstream code.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every required field that can be absent becomes an instruction to invent.
    ↳ Do instead: allow null, and let the downstream code decide what a missing value means.
  • Shelf life: provider limits are volatile (see the Landscape). A legal absent value and a checkable source won't date.

Connections

Path:output-format specificationJSON mode and schemasextractionparsing and repair loops
  • Builds on JSON mode and schemas: this note assumes the guarantee and works where it stops.
  • Owned elsewhere: structured output from RAG covers extraction over retrieved text.
  • Enforced by parsing and repair loops: what happens to a record that fails a check.
  • Used by multimodal prompting: the same contract over a page image.
  • Attacked by indirect prompt injection: the document is untrusted text in the window.
  • Measured by golden datasets: gold records and an absent-field cohort.

notes.title: Prompting for Summarisation — Faithful First, Short Second
notes.html:
References

Maynez et al. 2020: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization · Anthropic: reduce hallucinations

TL;DR

Summarising is a faithfulness problem before it is a length problem. A rewrite in new words can add what the source never said. So ask for a source span per claim, and let your code look the span up.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
Abstractive vs extractive? New words can invent; copied spans can't, though they can still mislead by omission.
Faithful vs relevant? Supported by the source, against worth including. One doesn't imply the other.
What still holds if the model ignores this? Only your span lookup; the instruction itself is a request.

The idea

A report summary states a figure the report never gave, and it reads fine. Maynez et al. (2020) found substantial hallucinated content in the summaries of every model they annotated. Ask for a quote per claim, and for "not covered" when the source is silent. A count of bullets is easier for code to check than a word limit. Length is owned by output length, chat histories by compression and history management, and retrieved answers by faithfulness.

Evolution

Lineage:May 2020 faithfulness measuredSep 2023 Chain of Density prompting. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): Anthropic still advises quotes and citations, and says they reduce hallucination without eliminating it.

notes.title: Classification at Scale — Closed Labels, a Way Out, the Smallest Output
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: batch processing · OpenAI: Batch API

TL;DR

At volume the prompt's job is label design: mutually exclusive classes, a stated tie-break, and an explicit "none of these". The bill is items × tokens per item, so the output stays one label, and anything that needn't be live goes to a batch API.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why a "none of these" class? Otherwise an item that fits nothing is forced into a wrong label.
Is invalid-label rate still a useful signal? Not under an enforced enum: it stays zero. Watch the "other" rate and label mix.
What does batch cost? 50% of standard on all three providers (Oct 2026).

The idea

cost = items × (input tokens · r_in + output tokens · r_out) × batch multiplier  ← r: price per token

A million tickets means every extra output token is multiplied a million times. Caution: on models that think by default, thinking counts toward max_tokens, so a cap sized for one label can cut the reply off. The enum is owned by schemas, label-token scoring by classification prompts, batch design by batch prompting.

Evolution

Lineage: 2024 enums enforced by schema moved the problem from parsing to label design. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).

notes.title: Cross-Lingual Prompting — Three Languages, Chosen Separately
notes.html:
References

Liu et al. 2024: Is Translation All You Need? · Anthropic: multilingual support

TL;DR

Three separate choices: the instruction language, the content language and the output language. State the output language explicitly. Whether English instructions beat native ones depends on the task and the model, so test in your target languages.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time

Recall

Prompt Answer
Do English instructions always win? No. They led on Arabic NLP tasks; native won on culture-related tasks.
Where to state the output language? Anthropic (Oct 2026): the system prompt, stable across turns.
Native script or transliteration? Native script, per Anthropic's guide.

The idea

A support bot tested in English answers Hindi users in English, because nobody stated the output language. Stating it fixes that request; it says nothing about quality. Kmainasi et al. (2024) found non-native prompts best on average across Arabic tasks; Liu et al. found native prompts better on culture-related tasks. Separately, Yong et al. (2023) reached 79% attack success on AdvBench with GPT-4 by translating into low-resource languages. Localised variants: multi-tenant prompts.

Evolution

Lineage:Oct 2022 MGSM2024 English-vs-native studiesApr 2026 CulturALL. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): results differ by model, so re-measure per language.
